module_title: Sizing Solar Systems for Different Business Types

lessons.title: Solar for a Small Retail Shop: Lights, Fridge, POS
lessons.body: A small retail shop in Africa typically needs power for LED lights, a refrigerator for cold drinks, and a point-of-sale (POS) machine or phone for mobile money. Start by listing each appliance and its wattage. For example: 5 LED bulbs at 10W each = 50W, one fridge at 150W (but it cycles on and off, so average 50W per hour), and a POS machine at 50W. Total running watts = 250W. But you must account for surge: the fridge compressor may surge to 600W for a few seconds. So your inverter must handle at least 600W continuous, but a 1kVA inverter (800W) is safer. For daily energy, multiply running watts by hours used. Lights: 50W Ã 6 hours = 300Wh. Fridge: 50W average Ã 24 hours = 1200Wh. POS: 50W Ã 8 hours = 400Wh. Total daily energy = 1900Wh (1.9kWh). To size the battery, decide how many days of backup you want. For one day, a 12V 200Ah battery gives 2400Wh (12Ã200=2400), but you should only discharge to 50% for lead-acid, so usable is 1200Wh â not enough. You need at least a 12V 400Ah battery or a 24V 200Ah system. For solar panels, assume 4 peak sun hours per day in most of Africa. To generate 1900Wh, you need 1900/4 = 475W of panels. Round up to 500W (e.g., two 250W panels). Use a 30A MPPT charge controller. Always add 20% safety margin. So final: 1kVA inverter, 24V 200Ah lithium battery (or 2Ã12V 200Ah lead-acid in series), 600W solar panels, 40A MPPT. Mount panels facing north (in southern hemisphere) or south (northern hemisphere) at angle equal to your latitude. Use proper DC cables and fuses. This system will keep your shop running through cloudy days if you manage loads carefully.

lessons.title: Solar for a Barbershop or Salon: Clippers, Fans, Music
lessons.body: A barbershop or salon uses clippers (50-100W each), fans (60-80W), music system (100W), and maybe a small water heater or hair dryer (1000-2000W). The hair dryer is the big load â if you use it frequently, you need a larger system. Start by listing all appliances and their wattages. Example: 2 clippers (100W), 2 fans (160W), music (100W), and one hair dryer (1500W). Total running watts if all on = 1860W. But you rarely run everything at once. For surge, the hair dryer and clippers may have motors that surge 2-3 times. So inverter should handle at least 3000W continuous. A 3kVA inverter (2400W) might be borderline; a 5kVA (4000W) is better. For daily energy, estimate hours: clippers 2h Ã 100W = 200Wh, fans 8h Ã 160W = 1280Wh, music 4h Ã 100W = 400Wh, hair dryer 1h Ã 1500W = 1500Wh. Total = 3380Wh (3.4kWh). Battery bank: for one day backup, use lithium to avoid 50% depth of discharge limit. A 24V 200Ah lithium gives 4800Wh usable. Or 48V 100Ah gives 4800Wh. Solar panels: 3380Wh / 4 sun hours = 845W. Round to 1000W (e.g., four 250W panels). Charge controller: 1000W / 24V = 41.7A, so use a 50A MPPT. If you use 48V, 1000W / 48V = 20.8A, use 30A MPPT. Wiring: use 6mmÂ² or 10mmÂ² DC cables for battery to inverter. Add a fuse or breaker on the battery positive. For the hair dryer, consider a separate inverter or run it only when sun is strong. Many salons in Africa use a 3kVA hybrid inverter with 24V 200Ah lithium and 1200W panels. That handles clippers, fans, music, and occasional hair dryer. Always teach staff to turn off unused appliances to save battery.

lessons.title: Solar for a Welding or Carpentry Workshop: High Surge Tools
lessons.body: Welding machines and carpentry tools like circular saws, planers, and compressors have very high surge currents. A typical welding machine draws 3000-5000W continuous and can surge to 8000W or more. A circular saw (1500W) may surge to 4500W. So you cannot use a small inverter. You need a heavy-duty inverter, often 48V or higher, with a continuous rating of at least 5000W and surge of 10000W. For a workshop, list all tools and their running watts. Example: welder 4000W, circular saw 1500W, drill 800W, lights 200W. But you rarely run all at once. Still, the welder alone needs 4000W continuous. So inverter should be 5kW continuous, 10kW surge. For daily energy, estimate hours: welder 2h Ã 4000W = 8000Wh, saw 1h Ã 1500W = 1500Wh, drill 1h Ã 800W = 800Wh, lights 4h Ã 200W = 800Wh. Total = 11100Wh (11.1kWh). Battery bank: use lithium for high discharge. A 48V 200Ah lithium gives 9600Wh usable. You might need two in parallel for 19.2kWh. Or use 48V 300Ah. Solar panels: 11100Wh / 4 sun hours = 2775W. Round to 3000W (twelve 250W panels). Charge controller: 3000W / 48V = 62.5A, so use an 80A MPPT. Wiring: use large cables, at least 25mmÂ² for battery to inverter, and proper fuses. For welders, consider a separate high-frequency inverter or a generator backup. Many workshops in Africa use a 5kVA hybrid inverter with 48V 200Ah lithium and 3000W panels, but they run the welder only during sunny hours and use a generator for heavy continuous welding. Always consult a professional for such high-power systems. Safety: ensure proper grounding and ventilation for batteries.

lessons.title: Solar for a Poultry Farm: Incubators, Lights, Water Pumps
lessons.body: A poultry farm needs constant power for incubators (critical), lights, and water pumps. Incubators are the most sensitive: they must run 24/7 and cannot lose power for more than a few hours. A typical small incubator uses 200-400W, but it cycles on and off, so average 100-200W. Lights: 10 LED bulbs at 10W = 100W, used 12 hours. Water pump: 500W, used 2 hours per day. List all loads. Example: incubator 300W (average 150W), lights 100W, pump 500W. Total running watts if all on = 900W. Surge: pump may surge to 1500W. So inverter should be at least 1.5kVA continuous, 3kVA surge. For daily energy: incubator 150W Ã 24h = 3600Wh, lights 100W Ã 12h = 1200Wh, pump 500W Ã 2h = 1000Wh. Total = 5800Wh (5.8kWh). Battery: for one day backup, use lithium. 48V 150Ah gives 7200Wh usable. Or 24V 300Ah gives 7200Wh. Solar panels: 5800Wh / 4 sun hours = 1450W. Round to 1600W (e.g., eight 200W panels). Charge controller: 1600W / 48V = 33.3A, use 40A MPPT. For incubators, you need a pure sine wave inverter to avoid damaging the thermostat. Also, consider a backup generator or a second battery bank for redundancy. In Africa, many poultry farms use a 3kVA hybrid inverter with 48V 200Ah lithium and 2000W panels. Water pumps can be run during sunny hours to save battery. Always monitor battery voltage and set a low-voltage cutoff to protect the battery. Incubators should have their own dedicated circuit. Use proper ventilation for the battery room.

lessons.title: Solar for a Phone Charging Kiosk: High Demand, Low Power
lessons.body: A phone charging kiosk typically has 10-20 charging ports, each drawing about 5-10W. So total running watts = 20 ports Ã 10W = 200W. But you also need lights (20W) and a fan (60W) for comfort. Total running watts = 280W. Surge is minimal because phone chargers are low-power. A 500W inverter is sufficient. For daily energy, estimate hours: charging ports used 8 hours Ã 200W = 1600Wh, lights 6h Ã 20W = 120Wh, fan 8h Ã 60W = 480Wh. Total = 2200Wh (2.2kWh). Battery: for one day backup, use lithium. 12V 200Ah lithium gives 2400Wh usable, but you need 2200Wh, so it's tight. Better to use 24V 100Ah lithium (2400Wh) or 12V 300Ah. Solar panels: 2200Wh / 4 sun hours = 550W. Round to 600W (e.g., three 200W panels). Charge controller: 600W / 12V = 50A, so use a 60A MPPT. If using 24V, 600W / 24V = 25A, use 30A MPPT. Wiring: use 6mmÂ² cables for battery to inverter. For phone charging, use USB ports that are efficient. Many kiosks in Africa use a 1kVA inverter with 12V 200Ah lithium and 600W panels. But if you have many customers, you might need more. Consider a 24V system for efficiency. Also, add a timer or coin-operated system to manage usage. Keep the battery in a cool place. Use a pure sine wave inverter to protect phones. This business has low power but high demand, so you can charge many phones simultaneously. Always have spare fuses and cables. Teach customers to bring their own cables to reduce wear.

lessons.title: Calculating Return on Investment for Your Solar Setup
lessons.body: To calculate ROI, you need to know your total system cost, your monthly savings from not buying fuel or grid electricity, and the system's lifespan. Start by adding up all costs: solar panels, inverter, batteries, charge controller, mounting, cables, and installation. For example, a small shop system (1kVA inverter, 24V 200Ah lithium, 600W panels) might cost $1500 in many African countries. Next, estimate your monthly energy savings. If you previously used a generator, calculate fuel cost per month. A small generator uses about 1 liter per hour, running 6 hours a day = 180 liters per month. At $1.2 per liter, that's $216 per month. If you used grid electricity, calculate your monthly bill for the same loads. Suppose you paid $50 per month. So savings = $216 - $50 = $166 per month if you switch from generator to solar. But with solar, you have no fuel cost, so savings = $216 per month. Now, ROI = total cost / monthly savings = $1500 / $216 = 6.94 months. That means the system pays for itself in about 7 months. After that, it's pure profit. However, you must account for battery replacement. Lithium batteries last 5-10 years, lead-acid 2-3 years. If you use lead-acid, you might replace them every 3 years at $400, so add that to annual cost. Also, consider maintenance and occasional inverter replacement. For a more accurate ROI, use the formula: ROI = (Total Cost + (Replacement Cost Ã Years)) / (Monthly Savings Ã 12 Ã Years). For example, over 5 years with lithium: total cost $1500, no replacement, savings $216Ã12Ã5 = $12,960. ROI = 1500/12960 = 0.116, or 11.6% per year. That's a good return. For a barbershop with a $3000 system saving $300 per month, ROI = 3000/300 = 10 months. Always include a 10% contingency for unexpected costs. Use a simple spreadsheet to compare. Many African businesses see ROI in 6-18 months. The key is to accurately measure your current energy expenses and size the system correctly to avoid overspending.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sizing Solar Systems for Different African Business Types

This reference lesson turns the six business scenarios in this module into a single, practical sizing and decision toolkit. Use it as a lookup sheet when a customer walks into your shop, when you quote a client, or when you check whether a proposed system will actually pay for itself. The numbers here are working estimates for African conditions: high ambient temperatures, variable grid quality, and equipment that is often imported and repaired locally rather than replaced.

The core rule for every business type is the same: size the battery bank around daily energy use, size the inverter around the single largest surge load, and size the panels around the worst month of sunshine. Most failed solar installations in Africa fail on one of those three points, not on the panel brand.

Table 1: Typical Daily Energy Demand by Business Type

Use this table to sanity-check a customer's claim about what they run. Figures assume a 12-hour trading day unless noted, and include a 25% system loss margin.

Business Type Typical Loads Est. Daily Energy (Wh) Suggested Battery (kWh) Inverter Size
Small retail shop 4 LED lights, 1 chest fridge, POS terminal, phone charging 2,000â3,500 3â5 1â1.5 kVA
Barbershop / salon 6 LED lights, 2 clippers, 2 fans, music system 1,200â2,000 2â3 0.8â1 kVA
Welding / carpentry Welder or bench saw, lights, grinder, radio 4,000â7,000 6â10 3â5 kVA
Poultry farm Incubator, brooder lights, water pump, ventilation 3,000â6,000 5â8 2â3 kVA
Phone charging kiosk 20â40 chargers, 2 lights, small fan 800â1,500 1.5â2.5 0.5â0.8 kVA

Source: Adapted from the Global Off-Grid Lighting Association (GOGLA) Consumer Protection and Quality Assurance guidance and the ESMAP Solar Market Trends data on productive-use appliance loads in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Table 2: Sizing Multipliers and Payback Indicators

These multipliers convert a load estimate into a purchase decision. Payback is calculated against the cost of the displaced energy source (grid, diesel, or kerosene) and is expressed in months for a typical urban or peri-urban African business.

Parameter Retail Barbershop Workshop Poultry Kiosk
Battery autonomy (days) 1.5 1.5 1.0 2.0 1.0
Depth of discharge (Li-ion) 80% 80% 70% 80% 80%
Panel oversizing factor 1.3 1.3 1.4 1.3 1.2
Peak sun hours (worst month) 4.0â5.5 across most of West, East, and Southern Africa
Typical payback (months) 18â30 14â24 24â40 20â36 8â16

Source: Payback ranges derived from the Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) Africa Solar Outlook and IRENA Renewable Power Generation Costs (2023), adjusted for typical commercial tariffs and diesel backup costs.

â  SAFETY WARNING â BATTERY AND WIRING HAZARDS

Never size a battery bank below the inverter's minimum DC input voltage, and never connect a lithium and lead-acid bank in parallel. In high-temperature African environments, battery rooms must be ventilated above 30Â°C and cables must be rated for the full surge current, not the running current. A welding workshop drawing 5 kVA surge through undersized DC cables is a fire risk, not a sizing error. Always install a DC circuit breaker and a surge protection device on the PV side.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • List every load, including phone chargers. Small loads left off the list are the most common cause of a system that runs flat by 6 p.m.
  • Measure surge, not just running watts. Fridges, pumps, welders, and saws decide your inverter size; lights and clippers do not.
  • Use worst-month peak sun hours. A system sized on the best month will fail in the cloudy season.
  • Add a 25% loss margin for heat, cable losses, dust on panels, and inverter efficiency.
  • Match battery chemistry to the business. Lithium for daily deep cycling (kiosk, retail); lead-acid only where budget forces it and maintenance is reliable.
  • Confirm the inverter's continuous and surge ratings separately before quoting. A 3 kVA inverter may only surge to 6 kVA for a few seconds.
  • Calculate payback against the real displaced cost â grid tariff, diesel per litre, or kerosene per week â not against a retail price you wish you could charge.
  • Plan for expansion. A retail shop today is a retail shop with a second fridge next year. Leave one spare breaker and 20% panel headroom.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • ESMAP / World Bank â Mini Grids for Half a Billion People (free handbook, includes load assessment and sizing chapters).
  • IRENA â Off-grid Renewable Energy Statistics and Renewable Power Generation Costs (free PDFs, Africa-specific cost and sizing data).
  • GOGLA â Consumer Protection and Quality Assurance Resources (free guidance on appliance loads and system quality for off-grid products).
  • Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) â Africa Solar Outlook (free annual outlook with market and payback context).
  • U.S. DOE Solar Energy Technologies Office â Solar Integration and Sizing Basics (free technical primers, useful for surge and inverter fundamentals).

Final business note: In African markets, the winning solar quote is rarely the cheapest one. It is the one where the battery, inverter, and panel sizes were each derived from the customer's actual daily load, and where the payback was shown in months against the energy cost the business already pays. Use the two tables above as your starting point, then adjust for local sun hours, tariff, and equipment availability.

quiz.q: What is the first step when sizing a solar system for a small retail shop?
options: A) Buy the largest inverter available
B) List all appliances and their wattages
quiz.explanation: Listing appliances and wattages is the foundation for accurate sizing.

quiz.q: For a small shop with a fridge, why must you consider surge power?
options: A) Because fridges use DC power
B) Because the compressor motor draws a high surge on startup
D) Because fridges are low power
quiz.explanation: The fridge compressor surges to 2-3 times its running wattage when starting.

quiz.q: If a shop needs 1900Wh daily and you get 4 peak sun hours, what size solar panel array is needed (before safety margin)?
quiz.explanation: Daily energy divided by peak sun hours: 1900Wh / 4h = 475W.

quiz.q: Why is a 12V 200Ah lead-acid battery often insufficient for a shop needing 1900Wh daily?
options: B) It can only be discharged to 50%, giving 1200Wh usable
C) It cannot power a fridge
quiz.explanation: Lead-acid batteries should not be discharged below 50% to avoid damage, so usable capacity is halved.

quiz.q: What is a safe inverter size for a barbershop with clippers, fans, music, and a hair dryer?
quiz.explanation: A hair dryer alone can draw 1500W, and surge from motors requires at least 3kVA.

quiz.q: In a salon, which appliance typically has the highest surge power?
quiz.explanation: Hair dryers have heating elements and motors that cause high surge currents.

quiz.q: If a barbershop needs 3380Wh daily and uses a 24V lithium battery, what minimum capacity is needed for one day backup?
quiz.explanation: 24V Ã 200Ah = 4800Wh, which covers 3380Wh with margin.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using lithium batteries for a salon with a hair dryer?
options: B) They can be discharged deeper without damage
C) They require no charge controller
D) They work only with 12V systems
quiz.explanation: Lithium batteries can be discharged to 80-100% depth, providing more usable energy.

quiz.q: Why do welding machines require a very large inverter?
options: B) They have high continuous and surge power demands
quiz.explanation: Welders draw 3000-5000W continuous and can surge to 8000W or more.

quiz.q: For a workshop with a 4000W welder, what should be the minimum inverter continuous rating?
quiz.explanation: The inverter must handle at least the welder's continuous draw, so 5000W is safe.

quiz.q: What is a recommended battery voltage for a high-surge workshop system?
quiz.explanation: Higher voltage reduces current and allows for more power with smaller cables.

quiz.q: If a workshop needs 11100Wh daily and gets 4 sun hours, what size solar array is needed?
Why is a pure sine wave inverter important for a poultry farm incubator?
options: B) It protects sensitive thermostats and motors
quiz.explanation: Modified sine wave can damage incubator controls; pure sine wave is safe.

quiz.q: In a poultry farm, which load is most critical and must run 24/7?
quiz.explanation: Incubators must maintain temperature constantly, so they need uninterrupted power.

quiz.q: If a poultry farm needs 5800Wh daily, what size battery (48V) is needed for one day backup?
quiz.explanation: 48V Ã 150Ah = 7200Wh, which covers 5800Wh with margin.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for water pumps in a solar poultry farm?
options: B) Run them during sunny hours
C) Run them only when battery is full
quiz.explanation: Running pumps during peak sun uses solar directly and saves battery.

quiz.q: For a phone charging kiosk with 20 ports at 10W each, what is the total running wattage?
quiz.explanation: 20 ports Ã 10W = 200W.

quiz.q: Why is a phone charging kiosk considered 'high demand, low power'?
options: A) Many customers but low wattage per device
B) Few customers but high wattage
quiz.explanation: Many phones can be charged at once, but each draws only a few watts.

quiz.q: If a kiosk needs 2200Wh daily, what size solar array is needed (4 sun hours)?
What is a recommended inverter size for a phone charging kiosk with 20 ports?
quiz.explanation: Total running watts is about 280W, so a 500W inverter is sufficient.

quiz.q: What is the formula for simple ROI in months?
options: C) Total cost Ã monthly savings
quiz.explanation: ROI in months = total system cost divided by monthly savings.

quiz.q: If a solar system costs $1500 and saves $216 per month, what is the ROI in months?
Why must you include battery replacement cost in ROI calculations?
options: B) Batteries have a limited lifespan and must be replaced
D) Batteries do not affect ROI
quiz.explanation: Lead-acid batteries last 2-3 years, so replacement adds to total cost over time.

quiz.q: What is a typical ROI period for a well-sized solar system for a small business in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Many businesses see payback in 6-18 months due to high fuel savings.

quiz.q: For a barbershop with a $3000 system saving $300 per month, what is the ROI in months?
What should you add to your ROI calculation for unexpected costs?
quiz.explanation: A 10% contingency covers minor unexpected expenses.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical load in a small retail shop?
quiz.explanation: Welding machines are high-power tools not found in a small shop.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to use a 24V or 48V system instead of 12V for larger loads?
options: A) Higher voltage reduces current and cable size
quiz.explanation: Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, allowing thinner cables and less loss.

quiz.q: For a poultry farm, why is a backup generator sometimes recommended?
options: B) To provide power during long cloudy periods
C) To run the incubator at night
D) To reduce solar panel size
quiz.explanation: Extended cloudy weather can deplete batteries, so a generator ensures incubator keeps running.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do before installing a solar system for any business?
options: C) Install panels on the roof
quiz.explanation: An energy audit identifies all loads and their usage patterns, which is essential for correct sizing.
